005package org.wpilib.math.filter;
006
007import java.util.Arrays;
008import org.ejml.simple.SimpleMatrix;
009import org.wpilib.util.UsageReporting;
010import org.wpilib.util.container.DoubleCircularBuffer;
011
012/**
013 * This class implements a linear, digital filter. All types of FIR and IIR filters are supported.
014 * Static factory methods are provided to create commonly used types of filters.
015 *
016 * <p>Filters are of the form: y[n] = (b0 x[n] + b1 x[n-1] + ... + bP x[n-P]) - (a0 y[n-1] + a2
017 * y[n-2] + ... + aQ y[n-Q])
018 *
019 * <p>Where: y[n] is the output at time "n" x[n] is the input at time "n" y[n-1] is the output from
020 * the LAST time step ("n-1") x[n-1] is the input from the LAST time step ("n-1") b0...bP are the
021 * "feedforward" (FIR) gains a0...aQ are the "feedback" (IIR) gains IMPORTANT! Note the "-" sign in
022 * front of the feedback term! This is a common convention in signal processing.
023 *
024 * <p>What can linear filters do? Basically, they can filter, or diminish, the effects of
025 * undesirable input frequencies. High frequencies, or rapid changes, can be indicative of sensor
026 * noise or be otherwise undesirable. A "low pass" filter smooths out the signal, reducing the
027 * impact of these high frequency components. Likewise, a "high pass" filter gets rid of slow-moving
028 * signal components, letting you detect large changes more easily.
029 *
030 * <p>Example FRC applications of filters: - Getting rid of noise from an analog sensor input -
031 * Smoothing out joystick input to prevent the wheels from slipping or the robot from tipping -
032 * Smoothing motor commands so that unnecessary strain isn't put on electrical or mechanical
033 * components - If you use clever gains, you can make a PID controller out of this class!
034 *
035 * <p>For more on filters, we highly recommend the following articles:<br>
036 * <a
037 * href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_filter">https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_filter</a>
038 * <br>
039 * <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iir_filter">https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iir_filter</a>
040 * <br>
041 * <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fir_filter">https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fir_filter</a>
042 * <br>
043 *
044 * <p>For IIR filters of order 4 or higher, prefer BiquadFilter — it represents the filter as a
045 * cascade of 2nd-order sections (Direct Form II Transposed), which avoids the numerical instability
046 * that high-order direct-form polynomials exhibit. Use LinearFilter for low-order IIR ({@code
047 * singlePoleIIR}, {@code highPass}) and FIR filters ({@code movingAverage}, {@code
048 * finiteDifference}).
049 *
050 * <p>Note 1: calculate() should be called by the user on a known, regular period. You can use a
051 * Notifier for this or do it "inline" with code in a periodic function.
052 *
053 * <p>Note 2: For ALL filters, gains are necessarily a function of frequency. If you make a filter
054 * that works well for you at, say, 100Hz, you will most definitely need to adjust the gains if you
055 * then want to run it at 200Hz! Combining this with Note 1 - the impetus is on YOU as a developer
056 * to make sure calculate() gets called at the desired, constant frequency!
057 */
058public class LinearFilter {
059  private final DoubleCircularBuffer m_inputs;
060  private final DoubleCircularBuffer m_outputs;
061  private final double[] m_inputGains;
062  private final double[] m_outputGains;
063  private double m_lastOutput;
064
065  private static int instances;
066
067  /**
068   * Create a linear FIR or IIR filter.
069   *
070   * @param ffGains The "feedforward" or FIR gains.
071   * @param fbGains The "feedback" or IIR gains.
072   */
073  public LinearFilter(double[] ffGains, double[] fbGains) {
074    m_inputs = new DoubleCircularBuffer(ffGains.length);
075    m_outputs = new DoubleCircularBuffer(fbGains.length);
076    m_inputGains = Arrays.copyOf(ffGains, ffGains.length);
077    m_outputGains = Arrays.copyOf(fbGains, fbGains.length);
078
079    instances++;
080    UsageReporting.reportUsage("LinearFilter", String.valueOf(instances));
081  }
082
083  /**
084   * Creates a one-pole IIR low-pass filter of the form: y[n] = (1-gain) x[n] + gain y[n-1] where
085   * gain = e<sup>-dt / T</sup>, T is the time constant in seconds.
086   *
087   * <p>Note: T = 1 / (2πf) where f is the cutoff frequency in Hz, the frequency above which the
088   * input starts to attenuate.
089   *
090   * <p>This filter is stable for time constants greater than zero.
091   *
092   * @param timeConstant The discrete-time time constant in seconds.
093   * @param period The period in seconds between samples taken by the user.
094   * @return Linear filter.
095   */
096  public static LinearFilter singlePoleIIR(double timeConstant, double period) {
097    double gain = Math.exp(-period / timeConstant);
098    double[] ffGains = {1.0 - gain};
099    double[] fbGains = {-gain};
100
101    return new LinearFilter(ffGains, fbGains);
102  }
103
104  /**
105   * Creates a first-order high-pass filter of the form: y[n] = gain x[n] + (-gain) x[n-1] + gain
106   * y[n-1] where gain = e<sup>-dt / T</sup>, T is the time constant in seconds.
107   *
108   * <p>Note: T = 1 / (2πf) where f is the cutoff frequency in Hz, the frequency below which the
109   * input starts to attenuate.
110   *
111   * <p>This filter is stable for time constants greater than zero.
112   *
113   * @param timeConstant The discrete-time time constant in seconds.
114   * @param period The period in seconds between samples taken by the user.
115   * @return Linear filter.
116   */
117  public static LinearFilter highPass(double timeConstant, double period) {
118    double gain = Math.exp(-period / timeConstant);
119    double[] ffGains = {gain, -gain};
120    double[] fbGains = {-gain};
121
122    return new LinearFilter(ffGains, fbGains);
123  }
124
125  /**
126   * Creates a K-tap FIR moving average filter of the form: y[n] = 1/k (x[k] + x[k-1] + ... + x[0]).
127   *
128   * <p>This filter is always stable.
129   *
130   * @param taps The number of samples to average over. Higher = smoother but slower.
131   * @return Linear filter.
132   * @throws IllegalArgumentException if number of taps is less than 1.
133   */
134  public static LinearFilter movingAverage(int taps) {
135    if (taps <= 0) {
136      throw new IllegalArgumentException("Number of taps was not at least 1");
137    }
138
139    double[] ffGains = new double[taps];
140    Arrays.fill(ffGains, 1.0 / taps);
141
142    double[] fbGains = new double[0];
143
144    return new LinearFilter(ffGains, fbGains);
145  }
146
147  /**
148   * Creates a finite difference filter that computes the nth derivative of the input given the
149   * specified stencil points.
150   *
151   * <p>Stencil points are the indices of the samples to use in the finite difference. 0 is the
152   * current sample, -1 is the previous sample, -2 is the sample before that, etc. Don't use
153   * positive stencil points (samples from the future) if the LinearFilter will be used for
154   * stream-based online filtering (e.g., taking derivative of encoder samples in real-time).
155   *
156   * @param derivative The order of the derivative to compute.
157   * @param stencil List of stencil points. Its length is the number of samples to use to compute
158   *     the given derivative. This must be one more than the order of the derivative or higher.
159   * @param period The period in seconds between samples taken by the user.
160   * @return Linear filter.
161   * @throws IllegalArgumentException if derivative &lt; 1, samples &lt;= 0, or derivative &gt;=
162   *     samples.
163   */
164  public static LinearFilter finiteDifference(int derivative, int[] stencil, double period) {
165    // See
166    // https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_difference_coefficient#Arbitrary_stencil_points
167    //
168    // For a given list of stencil points s of length n and the order of
169    // derivative d < n, the finite difference coefficients can be obtained by
170    // solving the following linear system for the vector a.
171    //
172    // [s₁⁰   ⋯  sₙ⁰ ][a₁]      [ δ₀,d ]
173    // [ ⋮    ⋱  ⋮   ][⋮ ] = d! [  ⋮   ]
174    // [s₁ⁿ⁻¹ ⋯ sₙⁿ⁻¹][aₙ]      [δₙ₋₁,d]
175    //
176    // where δᵢ,ⱼ are the Kronecker delta. The FIR gains are the elements of the
177    // vector 'a' in reverse order divided by hᵈ.
178    //
179    // The order of accuracy of the approximation is of the form O(hⁿ⁻ᵈ).
180
181    if (derivative < 1) {
182      throw new IllegalArgumentException(
183          "Order of derivative must be greater than or equal to one.");
184    }
185
186    int samples = stencil.length;
187
188    if (samples <= 0) {
189      throw new IllegalArgumentException("Number of samples must be greater than zero.");
190    }
191
192    if (derivative >= samples) {
193      throw new IllegalArgumentException(
194          "Order of derivative must be less than number of samples.");
195    }
196
197    var S = new SimpleMatrix(samples, samples);
198    for (int row = 0; row < samples; ++row) {
199      for (int col = 0; col < samples; ++col) {
200        S.set(row, col, Math.pow(stencil[col], row));
201      }
202    }
203
204    // Fill in Kronecker deltas: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_delta
205    var d = new SimpleMatrix(samples, 1);
206    for (int i = 0; i < samples; ++i) {
207      d.set(i, 0, (i == derivative) ? factorial(derivative) : 0.0);
208    }
209
210    var a = S.solve(d).divide(Math.pow(period, derivative));
211
212    // Reverse gains list
213    double[] ffGains = new double[samples];
214    for (int i = 0; i < samples; ++i) {
215      ffGains[i] = a.get(samples - i - 1, 0);
216    }
217
218    return new LinearFilter(ffGains, new double[0]);
219  }
220
221  /**
222   * Creates a backward finite difference filter that computes the nth derivative of the input given
223   * the specified number of samples.
224   *
225   * <p>For example, a first derivative filter that uses two samples and a sample period of 20 ms
226   * would be
227   *
228   * <pre><code>
229   * LinearFilter.backwardFiniteDifference(1, 2, 0.02);
230   * </code></pre>
231   *
232   * @param derivative The order of the derivative to compute.
233   * @param samples The number of samples to use to compute the given derivative. This must be one
234   *     more than the order of derivative or higher.
235   * @param period The period in seconds between samples taken by the user.
236   * @return Linear filter.
237   */
238  public static LinearFilter backwardFiniteDifference(int derivative, int samples, double period) {
239    // Generate stencil points from -(samples - 1) to 0
240    int[] stencil = new int[samples];
241    for (int i = 0; i < samples; ++i) {
242      stencil[i] = -(samples - 1) + i;
243    }
244
245    return finiteDifference(derivative, stencil, period);
246  }
247
248  /** Reset the filter state. */
249  public void reset() {
250    m_inputs.clear();
251    m_outputs.clear();
252  }
253
254  /**
255   * Resets the filter state, initializing internal buffers to the provided values.
256   *
257   * <p>These are the expected lengths of the buffers, depending on what type of linear filter used:
258   *
259   * <table>
260   * <tr><th>Type</th><th>Input Buffer Length</th><th>Output Buffer Length</th></tr>
261   * <tr><td>Unspecified</td><td>length of {@code ffGains}</td><td>length of {@code fbGains}</td>
262   * </tr>
263   * <tr><td>Single Pole IIR</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr>
264   * <tr><td>High-Pass</td><td>2</td><td>1</td></tr>
265   * <tr><td>Moving Average</td><td>{@code taps}</td><td>0</td></tr>
266   * <tr><td>Finite Difference</td><td>length of {@code stencil}</td><td>0</td></tr>
267   * <tr><td>Backward Finite Difference</td><td>{@code samples}</td><td>0</td></tr>
268   * </table>
269   *
270   * @param inputBuffer Values to initialize input buffer.
271   * @param outputBuffer Values to initialize output buffer.
272   * @throws IllegalArgumentException if length of inputBuffer or outputBuffer does not match the
273   *     length of ffGains and fbGains provided in the constructor.
274   */
275  public void reset(double[] inputBuffer, double[] outputBuffer) {
276    // Clear buffers
277    reset();
278
279    if (inputBuffer.length != m_inputGains.length || outputBuffer.length != m_outputGains.length) {
280      throw new IllegalArgumentException("Incorrect length of inputBuffer or outputBuffer");
281    }
282
283    for (double input : inputBuffer) {
284      m_inputs.addFirst(input);
285    }
286    for (double output : outputBuffer) {
287      m_outputs.addFirst(output);
288    }
289  }
290
291  /**
292   * Calculates the next value of the filter.
293   *
294   * @param input Current input value.
295   * @return The filtered value at this step
296   */
297  public double calculate(double input) {
298    double retVal = 0.0;
299
300    // Rotate the inputs
301    if (m_inputGains.length > 0) {
302      m_inputs.addFirst(input);
303    }
304
305    // Calculate the new value
306    for (int i = 0; i < m_inputGains.length; i++) {
307      retVal += m_inputs.get(i) * m_inputGains[i];
308    }
309    for (int i = 0; i < m_outputGains.length; i++) {
310      retVal -= m_outputs.get(i) * m_outputGains[i];
311    }
312
313    // Rotate the outputs
314    if (m_outputGains.length > 0) {
315      m_outputs.addFirst(retVal);
316    }
317
318    m_lastOutput = retVal;
319    return retVal;
320  }
321
322  /**
323   * Returns the last value calculated by the LinearFilter.
324   *
325   * @return The last value.
326   */
327  public double lastValue() {
328    return m_lastOutput;
329  }
330
331  /**
332   * Factorial of n.
333   *
334   * @param n Argument of which to take factorial.
335   */
336  private static int factorial(int n) {
337    if (n < 2) {
338      return 1;
339    } else {
340      return n * factorial(n - 1);
341    }
342  }
343}
